note: Hidden reference values and scoring parameters. Participants never see this file. Every entry carries a provenance tag: 'empirical' = a published figure is used directly, 'derived' = computed from published figures plus a stated assumption, 'placeholder' = needs the team's own interview or pilot data before fielding.

contest_rule.note: T2 and F2 in the walkthrough of 5 October already follow this rule exactly. The harmonised variant applies it to H2 and G2 as well, so that entry rates are comparable across the four domains (requirement R2, Section 6.3).

T1.quantity: share of the MVP built in-house
T1.basis: Two founders and five core features. Commercial MVP timelines of three to four months assume a team working on the MVP full time; a two-person founding team is also running fundraising, hiring and go-to-market in the same window. Committing the whole build in-house therefore assumes capacity the team does not have, which is the inside view of Kahneman and Lovallo (1993) and the planning fallacy of Buehler, Griffin and Ross (1994).
sources: Netguru MVP timeline guide (industry): MVP typically three to four months
Buehler, Griffin and Ross (1994)
Kahneman and Lovallo (1993)
T1.open: Confirm the reference step against the founder interviews before fielding.

T2.basis: Rank contest with an independent jury, after Camerer and Lovallo (1999) and the market entry game of Moore and Cain (2007). With ten teams and no information about rank the average team wins with probability 0.10, so both entry options have a negative expected value and entry signals a belief of being above average.
sources: Camerer and Lovallo (1999)
Moore and Cain (2007): entry 61 percent under random rank, 71 percent under a simple quiz, 42 percent under a difficult quiz, 91 participants
T2.display_note: Since 0.7.0 the screen states that an average startup has a 1 in 10 chance and that the upgrade raises it to 1 in 8, so the expected values of -2,000 and -4,500 euros are computable for everyone. Entry is a bet on being above average.

T3.quantity: weeks until the MVP is ready, five core features, two developers
T3.basis: Median anchored on commercial MVP timelines of three to four months. The spread is right-skewed, following the software schedule literature: effort and schedule overruns are common and the upper tail is long. Since 0.7.0 the question states the assumption (the equivalent of 2 full-time developers), so all participants estimate against the same plan.
sources: Netguru MVP timeline guide (industry): about four months
Joergensen (2004), A review of studies on expert estimation of software development effort
Buehler, Griffin and Ross (1994)
Flyvbjerg and Budzier (2011), Why your IT project may be riskier than you think, HBR: 1,471 IT projects, average cost overrun 27 percent, one in six projects overran by 200 percent
T3.open: If the interviews give MVP durations for comparable teams, replace the percentiles with that distribution.

F1.quantity: months of delay before the raise starts
F1.basis: The scored quantity is the runway left when the raise starts. An active seed process runs about two to three months, successful seed founders in the DocSend sample held about 40 investor meetings, and a first attempt that fails needs a second. Nine months of runway remaining is the reference; starting with less assumes a fast round. Since 0.7.0 the months until the chosen start are paid from cash when the round money arrives (F4), so the choice has a consequence. The reference is computed from the runway shown in the question (runway_shown in the snapshot), which is the runway at the start of the area.
sources: Elad Gil: a round takes about two to three months; start a round with at least six months of cash
DocSend seed report, 175 seed-stage startups: successful founders contacted 77 investors and held about 40 meetings
Buehler, Griffin and Ross (1994)
F1.open: The nine-month reference is a convention, not a measured distribution. Either defend it from the interviews or report the score for both a six- and a nine-month reference.

F2.basis: Same structure as T2, now framed as an accelerator selection so that it does not repeat the pitch contest of the first area. The prize is a grant, no equity taken, so the expected value is not affected by dilution.
sources: Camerer and Lovallo (1999)
Cain, Moore and Haran (2015)
F2.display_note: Since 0.7.0 the screen states that an average startup has a 1 in 10 chance and that the upgrade raises it to 1 in 8, so the expected values of -2,000 and -4,500 euros are computable for everyone. Entry is a bet on being above average.

F3.quantity: monthly revenue in 12 months, from 8,000 euros now
F3.basis: SaaS Capital 2025 benchmarking of private B2B SaaS companies, band below 1 million ARR: median annual growth 40 percent, 25th percentile 20 percent, 75th percentile 100 percent. Applied to the current 8,000 euros these give 11,200, 9,600 and 16,000 euros. The 10th and 90th percentiles are extrapolated as -10 percent and +200 percent. Note that naive extrapolation of the shown series (9, 14 and 6 percent) gives about 24,000 euros, which lands on the 90th percentile of the reference rather than at its centre.
sources: SaaS Capital (2025), Benchmarking Private SaaS Company Growth Rates, more than 1,000 respondents
ChartMogul SaaS Growth Report 2023, more than 2,200 SaaS businesses: median monthly growth 2 to 2.5 percent across the lifecycle
Cassar (2010)
F3.open: The 10th and 90th percentiles are extrapolated beyond the published quartiles. State this in the codebook appendix.
F3.scale_note: If GTM comes before Finance (Track 2), revenue at the start of Finance can exceed 8,000 euros. The chart and the question then show the actual revenue, and the answers are divided by revenue_shown / 8,000 before scoring, so the reference distribution keeps its meaning as a growth multiple.

F4.prediction: Higher overestimation scores make option A, the bank loan, more likely (Landier and Thesmar 2009; Malmendier, Tate and Yan 2011). Options in 0.5.0: loan, SAFE at a 6M cap, priced round of 5 percent with about 15,000 euros legal costs. SAFE terms follow Carta's pre-seed data, where most rounds are raised on SAFEs.

H1.quantity: roles opened in the next three months
H1.basis: Ashby's hiring benchmarks (press release of 7 May 2026, 100M+ applications, 200K+ jobs) put time to first fill at about 10 weeks for technical roles and about 8 weeks for business roles, against a 13-week window. A two-founder team without a recruiter can realistically close about two roles in that window; three or more assume several searches closing inside one typical time-to-fill. The DHI-DFH vacancy duration measure for the Information sector (30 to 46 working days) points the same way.
sources: Ashby, press release 7 May 2026: time to first fill about 10 weeks technical, about 8 weeks business
DHI-DFH Mean Vacancy Duration Measure, Information industry (FRED series DHIDFHDMII)
Buehler, Griffin and Ross (1994)
H1.open: Options 0 to 6 or more (scored as 6). Since 0.7.0 each new hire adds 5,000 euros to monthly costs when they join at the end of the Team area; four or more joining at once lower morale by 1.

H2.basis: Harmonised with T2 and F2 so that entry rates are comparable across domains. The walkthrough version used eight competitors, a 30,000 euro saving and an upgrade to one in five, which gave an expected value of -1,250 and -4,000 instead of -2,000 and -4,500. The upgrade is a higher salary and signing bonus, not equity, for the same reason.
sources: Camerer and Lovallo (1999)
Cain, Moore and Haran (2015)
H2.display_note: Since 0.7.0 the screen states that an average startup has a 1 in 10 chance and that the upgrade raises it to 1 in 8, so the expected values of -2,000 and -4,500 euros are computable for everyone. Entry is a bet on being above average.

H3.quantity: weeks from the start of the search to a signed contract
H3.basis: Ashby reports about 10 weeks from opening to first fill for technical roles (May 2026), close to the 11-week median used here. The DHI-DFH figure of 30 to 46 working days sets the fast end at roughly 5 to 8 calendar weeks. The right tail covers searches that stall or restart. The question names a senior backend engineer.
sources: Ashby, press release 7 May 2026
DHI-DFH Mean Vacancy Duration Measure, Information industry

H4.prediction: Higher overprecision scores make option B, the gut-feeling hire, more likely (Kausel, Culbertson and Madrid 2016; Dawes, Faust and Meehl 1989). Since 0.7.0 the order in which the two candidates are described is randomised (screen field 'first'); key A is always the work-sample candidate, B the gut-feeling candidate.

G1.quantity: share of the launch budget committed to the first channel
G1.basis: At Microsoft about one third of tested ideas prove effective, one third are neutral and one third are negative; at Google and Bing only 10 to 20 percent of experiments produce positive results. An untested first channel idea therefore has a base rate well below one half, so committing the whole budget to it assumes a hit rate far above the documented one. Chen, Elfenbein, Posen and Wang (2024) make the same argument for programs of experimentation.
sources: Kohavi and Thomke (2017), The Surprising Power of Online Experiments, Harvard Business Review
Chen, Elfenbein, Posen and Wang (2024)
Kahneman and Lovallo (1993)
G1.open: reference_value 0.40 leans on the 10 to 20 percent figure; the alternative 0.55 leans on the one-third figure alone. Report the sensitivity.

G2.basis: Harmonised with T2 and F2. The walkthrough version used a 150,000 euro contract with costs of 20,000 and 40,000, which gave an expected value of -5,000 and -21,250, far below the other three contests.
sources: Camerer and Lovallo (1999)
Moore, Oesch and Zietsma (2007)
G2.display_note: Since 0.7.0 the screen states that an average startup has a 1 in 10 chance and that the upgrade raises it to 1 in 8, so the expected values of -2,000 and -4,500 euros are computable for everyone. Entry is a bet on being above average.

G3.quantity: new paying customers from the pilot channel over the following six months, after 40, 65 and 90
G3.basis: New-customer inflow from a pilot channel flattens rather than continuing to rise linearly. The median path holds roughly the last observed monthly level and then decays, giving about 540 over six months. Naive linear extrapolation of the series gives 1,065, which sits above the 90th percentile of the reference.
sources: ChartMogul SaaS Growth Report 2023: growth rates decay with scale; the median early-stage company had flat year-on-year new business ARR
SaaS Capital (2025): median growth falls from 40 percent below 1M ARR to 20 percent above 20M ARR
G3.open: Weakest of the eight. The decay shape is an assumption, not a measured distribution. Anchor it on the founder interviews or on the team's own pilot data before fielding.

T5.basis: Belief about one's own rank among the 10 entrants of the contest that follows, asked before the entry decision. With no information about the others, the expected rank of an average entrant is 5.5. Score = 5.5 minus the stated rank, positive meaning a belief of being above average. This is the belief component of overplacement (Moore and Healy 2008; Benoit, Dubra and Moore 2015) and separates it from risk attitude, which also drives contest entry (Camerer and Lovallo 1999).
sources: Moore and Healy (2008), The trouble with overconfidence
Benoit, Dubra and Moore (2015), Does the better-than-average effect show that people are overconfident?
Camerer and Lovallo (1999), Overconfidence and excess entry

AC1.note: Instructed response in the question text; placed in area 2 of the track, never first.

AC2.note: Multiple selection; passed only if exactly E is selected. Placed in area 3, never first.

G4.prediction: Higher overestimation and overprecision scores make option A (stay the course) more likely and option C (a structured test) less likely: confident founders discount disconfirming early evidence and escalate commitment to their first plan. Chen, Elfenbein, Posen and Wang (2024) on programs of experimentation; Kirtley and O'Mahony (2023) on when entrepreneurial firms pivot.
sources: Chen, Elfenbein, Posen and Wang (2024)
Kirtley and O'Mahony (2023), What is a pivot?, Strategic Management Journal

K1.basis: Random-outcome control contest, the luck condition of Camerer and Lovallo (1999). Same prize, costs and expected values as F2 (-2,000 and -4,500 euros), but the winner is drawn by lot, so own skill cannot matter. Entry here reflects risk attitude only. The difference between entry in the four skill contests and entry in K1 is the overplacement component of contest entry. K1 is not part of the overplacement index; it is a within-person control variable. Asked after all four areas, same position for everyone.
sources: Camerer and Lovallo (1999), Overconfidence and excess entry
Moore and Cain (2007), random-rank condition

expected_hit_rate_literature.source: Soll and Klayman (2004), Overconfidence in interval estimates. The instrument uses the two-point format, asking the optimistic and the pessimistic value on separate screens, which in their data gave 57 percent against a target of 80 percent.
expected_hit_rate_literature.software_source: Joergensen (2004), Eliminating over-confidence in software development effort estimates: 62 percent hit rate for requested 90 percent intervals, 195 student project activities.

scoring.note: Overestimation and overplacement scores are signed so that positive means more aggressive than the reference. Overprecision uses the width ratio, where below 1 means narrower than the reference, plus the expected coverage of the reference distribution by the participant's interval.

display_rules.status_strip: The strip on decision screens shows the situation at the start of the area and does not move with decisions inside the area (team decision, 18 October). The current state before every answer is stored in state_json as the control variable.
display_rules.launch_budget: G1 uses a quarter of the cash at the start of the area, so the number in the question matches the strip.
display_rules.net_burn: Costs 28,000, revenue 8,000 (90 customers at about 89 euros each), net burn 20,000, runway 14 months. Revenue follows customers.
display_rules.popover: Removed in 0.8.0. The scientific background appears on hover over a link icon next to the question, author and year only. Assumptions a participant needs are written into the question text.
display_rules.industry: The industry chosen at setup is a label in the text only. All reference values assume a digital product.
display_rules.startup: Every participant runs the same fictional startup, Lumora. Solo or co-founders is taken from the team composition given in the demographics; the industry is chosen at setup (pre-selected from the participant's own industry) and used as a label only.

shown_background.note: What participants see on hover over the link icon, author and year only (team decision, 20 October).
